title: No away fans for Old Firm games this season after agreement reached
description: There will be no away supporters for Celtic and Rangers derbies in the Scottish Premiership or Premier Sports Cup this season.
fullText:
There will be no away supporters for Celtic and Rangers derbies in the Scottish Premiership or Premier Sports Cup this season.

The "temporary arrangement" was reached following talks between the Glasgow clubs and the Scottish Professional Football League (SPFL).

It follows the Scottish FA's independent review into events surrounding last term's Scottish Cup quarter-final at Ibrox, which was marred by unrest and pitch incursions from both sets of fans.

Rangers host Celtic in the Premier Sports Cup on 13 September, with the city rivals meeting at Celtic Park in the league a week later.

Rangers had proposed a reduced away allocation of 300 for the impending cup tie, with Celtic rejecting the offer.

The crowd disorder on 8 March came after a penalty shootout win for Celtic, when around 8,000 visiting supporters had been present.

That figure was much larger than recent Old Firm league derbies, with ticketing rules different for the Scottish Cup.

The Scottish FA announced last month that both clubs would have to play their next Scottish Cup home games behind closed doors.

Announcing the measures, a statement from the SPFL said: "This temporary arrangement will allow both clubs, together with the SPFL, Police Scotland and other relevant stakeholders, to give proper consideration to the findings and recommendations of the independent review, take forward the necessary actions and ensure sufficient time is available to plan future fixtures thoroughly.

"It will also provide greater certainty for supporters and those involved in matchday planning, while avoiding repeated uncertainty around ticketing arrangements for individual fixtures.

"All parties have committed to working constructively during this period, with safety and security remaining the priority."

The March cup meeting was the first time Celtic supporters have been given the full Broomloan Road Stand allocation at Ibrox since away allocations were reduced to fewer than 1,000 in 2018.

The number of away fans at both Ibrox and Celtic Park fluctuated between about 800 and zero in a series of tit-for-tat moves before an arrangement was reached for "around 5%" capacity [2,500 - 3,000] for league games in 2025 and 2026.

Rangers manager Derek McInnes described the news as "disappointing", saying: "It's always better when opposition fans are allowed into a derby game.

"In the context of everything that's gone on with this fixture and the last part of it, I think there's a lot to consider and a lot to discuss.

"As far as I was led to believe, that was still up for discussion, so it's kind of caught me on the hop a wee bit."

Celtic manager Martin O'Neill described the decision as "inevitable" and "really sad".

O'Neill added: "It's a great, great fixture when the ground is absolutely full. And I think the away fans make this.

"Hopefully the two clubs will maybe get together at some stage or another and try to iron out the particular problems."

title: Trio of Iowa football legends named to USA TODAY's all-2000s team
description: A trio of Iowa football legends were named to USA TODAY Sports' all-2000s team.
fullText:
The Iowa football program has seen many great players don the black and gold over the past 25 years.

The Kirk Ferentz era has brought a ton of success on and off the field for the Hawkeyes. Great players have led to wins and the most prosperous, sustained period of Iowa football ever. Even among all the greats, there are certain guys that stand out among the pack.

USA TODAY Sports identified a trio of Hawks from the Ferentz era who differentiated themselves from the rest. Writers Paul Myerberg, Eddie Timanus and Craig Meyer put together their All-2000's college football teams. The two teams consist of the best college football players from the dawn of the century until right now. Mixed in among the two teams were three Iowa football legends.

Iowa had one representative on the All-2000's first team: punter Tory Taylor. The writers had the following to say about the fan-favorite Aussie:

"Perhaps no program's fans appreciate their punter more than Iowa's, and few did it better than Taylor. The 2023 Ray Guy Award winner helped the Hawkeyes to a 10-3 record as a senior despite the team averaging just 16.6 points a game. Taylor averaged 46.3 yards per punt over his career and led the Bowl Subdivision in kicks downed inside the 20 three years in a row."

Two more Hawkeyes appeared on the All-2000's second team: tight end Dallas Clark and kicker Nate Kaeding. Clark was a mainstay on Iowa's offense for both the 2001 and 2002 seasons. Across those two years, he compiled 81 career receptions for 1,281 yards and eight touchdowns. He was named an All-American in 2002 and went on to be a first-round pick in the 2003 NFL Draft.

Kaeding is Iowa's career scoring leader with 373 points. The 2002 recipient of the Lou Groza Award, Kaeding was also a consensus All-American following his standout 2003 season. Kaeding made 67 field goals in his Hawkeye career and booted through 22 consecutive kicks at one point spanning the 2001 and 2002 seasons.

title: Astros' AL West dominance may face a $4 billion threat in Southern California
description: The Astros' longtime divisional punching bag just gained one of the richest and most accomplished owners in sports.
fullText:
The Houston Astros have essentially owned the American League West for a decade now, winning seven division titles, four American League pennants and two World Series championships. However, the Astros' divisional dominance could be up for grabs, as the organization must manage an aging roster and a likely need for new leadership in multiple positions.

On Tuesday, a new threat entered the proverbial AL West chat, with a resume that features a championship-winning pedigree across every major sport on two continents.

Billionaire team owner Stan Kroenke and Kroenke Sports Entertainment (KSE) entered into a definitive agreement on Tuesday to purchase the Los Angeles Angels from the Arte Moreno family for a reported MLB-record $4 billion. The transaction is expected to close in early 2027.

"The Angels are a storied franchise anchored in a great market," Kroenke said in a statement released by both the Angels and Kroenke Sports & Entertainment. "We look forward to an exciting future with the Angels organization."

Kroenke, who owns four franchises across four leagues, will likely bring a fresh perspective to a franchise that's been moribund and listless. The Angels are on track to miss the postseason for the 12th straight year and have essentially wasted the prime years of two of the best baseball talents of a generation in Shohei Ohtani and Mike Trout.

Under Kroenke's leadership, his teams have all won titles in the past five years, including:

English Premier League's Arsenal, 2026

A championship standard is now attainable KSE's as foundation for success, not just an aspirational one. Josh Kroenke, Arsenal's co-chairman, demonstrated these aspirations when hiring Andrea Berta as the club's new sporting director.

"I went to Andrea, and I laid out our championship rings," Josh Kroenke said to James Benge of CBS in May. "I said: 'This is what we're here for. So as we start to shape our thinking, know this is what we're going for.' He was looking at them pretty close!"

KSE isn't simply purchasing a baseball team; they're buying back into Southern California in an area that's highly valuable yet wholly undeveloped in Orange County. Kroenke's institutional knowledge means there is a real possibility of turning an aging ballpark and sports district into another year-round real estate and entertainment engine.

"The addition of the Angels to the KSE portfolio creates the opportunity for a year-round Southern California calendar of events," reads a statement from KSE on their future strategy.

The Angels sit on land-currently owned by the City of Anaheim-that could ultimately be more valuable than the team itself. Angel Stadium sits on approximately 150 acres, with surrounding areas potentially up for grabs. In fact, KSE recently developed SoFi Stadium as the anchor of a 300-acre Hollywood Park entertainment district focused on retail, offices, residences and hotels.

The Angels' reputation has suffered greatly under previous ownership, as the squandering of talents like Ohtani and Moreno has coincided with reports of downsizing in scouting, development and organizational resources. KSE's ownership has continually focused on stadium upgrades, revamped clubhouses, sports science investment and family-friendly facilities for players.

That type of resource commitment is enough to attract marquee players to any organization, but offering a Southern California lifestyle that includes year-round good weather, access to beaches, major entertainment opportunities, and increased endorsement potential can be a big joker in negotiations.

"Kroenke's got a track record of success and winning championships with his teams," Trout said to reporters on Tuesday. "I'm super excited about it and can't wait to meet him."

Just ask the Los Angeles Dodgers about offering such a benefit to free agents.

The Astros already booted their general manager in August, and Joe Espada's tenure as manager is clearly in doubt. Moreover, Astros owner Jim Crane has already shown hesitancy to spend big, instead relying on a cautious, methodical approach.

That strategy served the Astros well during their title-winning run, as their roster was stacked with future Hall of Famers and a minor league system stocked with future All-Stars. The club also featured rising stars in various leadership positions that proved to be innovative (and at times, too clever) before moving on to other teams. Playing in a warm-weather city with lucrative tax benefits has always been a plus, but for some, playing in Southern California has an appeal all its own.

The AL West includes teams that are either resource-rich but inconsistent, like the Seattle Mariners and Texas Rangers, or struggling significantly, such as the Athletics and Angels. In this environment, being consistently competent has been key to success, as the Astros have demonstrated for over a decade. But 2026 has proven how low the bar is for competency.

"The reality is no AL West team really deserves to reach the postseason this year. All five teams deserve to go home at the end of September," Yahoo MLB insider Russell Dorsey said in August. "But it doesn't work that way in baseball. So we all have to resign ourselves to watching maybe the saddest division race MLB has ever seen."

The Astros have a 138-89 record against the Angels since joining the AL West in 2013, but competency has now landed in Southern California. The Astros should prepare themselves accordingly.

title: Angels’ Outfield Depth in Trouble After Josh Lowe Injury Scratch
description: The Los Angeles Angels scratched outfielder Josh Lowe from Wednesday's game against the New York Yankees with neck stiffness. The post Angels’ Outfield Depth in Trouble After Josh Lowe Injury Scratch appeared first on LA Sports Report.
fullText:
The Los Angeles Angels scratched outfielder Josh Lowe from Wednesday's game against the New York Yankees with neck stiffness.

The Angels' outfield is severely lacking in depth, as they currently have just four outfielders listed on their active roster—one of whom is Lowe. Wade Meckler will move over to right field to cover for Lowe, with Jose Siri getting the start in left field.

Lowe, an offseason acquisition from the Tampa Bay Rays, has been with the Angels for nearly the entire season, only being away from the team during a month-long stint in Triple-A. He can play any position across the outfield, providing valuable depth in each position for the Halos.

The 28-year-old has 10 homers on the year, driving in 27 runs through 95 games this season. He has a .625 OPS this season, which would be the lowest mark of his career if he finishes the season at this pace.

His best stretch of baseball came after the Angels recalled him from Triple-A in June, where he went 8-for-18 through his final six games of June. He hit a homer and drove in four runs during that stretch, posting an OPS north of 1.000 during his hot streak.

Siri, Meckler and Mike Trout are the only other players explicitly listed as outfielders on the Angels' roster, though they have other players who could stand in if needed.

Other than Lowe, Siri, Meckler and Trout, the Angels have a few options if they need to bring someone into the outfield later in the year.

Kyren Paris came up from Triple-A Tuesday for the Angels' September call-ups, and he has plenty of experience in the outfield despite primarily playing in the middle of the infield. 2024 first-round pick Christian Moore also primarily plays in the infield, but the Angels tested him out in left field when they called him up earlier in the season.

Lastly, Adam Frazier has spent some time in the outfield this season for the Angels, and could fill in if needed.

Even still, the Angels' outfield is running extremely thin, and remains an area they'll have to reinforce come the offseason.

title: Tom Brady's sports memorabilia store to open in downtown Indianapolis
description: CardVault by Tom Brady will open at a central downtown corner this fall, bringing the former quarterback's brand to Indiana.
fullText:
Tom Brady will be setting up shop in Indianapolis. No, not on the football team.

CardVault by Tom Brady, a sports and trading cards, collectibles and memorabilia shop co-founded by the former Patriots quarterback, will open at 2 W. Washington St. in downtown Indianapolis later this year, said Nick Wright, who leases retail spaces on the building's ground floor.

The company signed a 10-year lease in the building known as the H.P. Wasson & Company Building.

CardVault leadership wants to open the Indianapolis store as soon as possible, Wright said. The initial plans called for opening by the first Colts home game, slated for Sunday, Sept. 13, but that's not likely to happen.

Wright deferred IndyStar to CardVault for more specific information on the grand opening, which Wright said Brady will likely attend. IndyStar's attempts to contact CardVault before publication were unsuccessful.

CardVault was established during the pandemic in 2020. Since then, the brand has become one of the fastest growing collectibles retail stores in the country, opening in "major cities near iconic venues," according to CardVault's website.

Currently, CardVault operates 17 brick-and-mortar stores alongside a handful of vending machine operations in Los Angeles, Boston and Minneapolis, where it sells sports memorabilia and trading cards brands, such as Pokémon. Inside, collectors can also submit items for grading.

CardVault's rise builds on a booming, multi-billion-dollar collectibles industry that has brought increased attention to the hobby of sports and trading cards. The industry is projected to be worth nearly $7 billion by 2035.

The store's spot in Indianapolis taps into the dedicated sports community, the annual presence of Gen Con at the convention center and regional sports shows, like the National Sports Collectors Convention held in Chicago earlier this summer.

Across the country, CardVault has been experimenting with setting up shop in downtown areas.

"It'll be a great place for people to get together and trade," Wright said of the Indianapolis store. "I'm really, really looking forward to seeing collectors, sports fans, visitors come together in this space. It's good for downtown and the growing collectibles industry."

The storefront on the northwest corner of the Meridian and Washington streets intersection has not been available for nearly two decades, Wright said. T-Mobile moved out of the space earlier this month. When the company moved out, Wright wanted to veer away from the typical coffee shop or restaurant space, aiming to bring an "experiential" store to the high-trafficked and visible corner.

Wright described CardVault as a win-win for downtown retail and the collectibles industry in Indianapolis.

"It says a lot about Indianapolis," Wright said.

title: Charlie Baker: When NFL, NBA players return to campus, everyone else pays the price
description: All four Power Conferences have signed off on the Protect College Sports Act. NCAA President Charlie Baker writes why it must be passed into law.
fullText:
The notion college sports are for college students who will move on when they complete their degree or turn pro enjoys near-universal support. But right now, that fundamental boundary is being dismantled amid a relentless wave of litigation.

In two cases, the NCAA has been ordered to allow professional basketball players to return to college basketball, despite the fact they intentionally left college to go to the NBA Draft and each played in several NBA games. In another case, a judge required the NCAA to allow an athlete to compete for a fifth school in five years. And in the past two weeks, without so much as a hearing, let alone a trial, two courts permitted NFL players to return immediately to college football. These few examples are merely the tip of the iceberg.

POWER PLAY: College football's 25 most powerful people

OP-ED: Federal antitrust protection is only workable path to saving college sports

Eligibility rules have long held a simple purpose: Ensuring a fair playing field while preserving access to the life-changing benefits college sports provide to actual college students. For decades, that standard meant allowing student-athletes four seasons of competition over five years. Recognizing the need for evolution, NCAA member schools recently updated this rule to allow up to five years of competition before age 24. However, since the start of 2025, more than 165 lawsuits have been filed seeking to tear down these basic limits.

As rosters are increasingly packed with older adults and former professionals, the most obvious consequence is an unfair matchup on the field. But the longer-term impact falls on the next generation of young athletes who will be squeezed out of the system as a result. Sidelining incoming freshmen doesn't just rob them of their roster spots or athletic scholarship opportunities — it also strips away their chance to experience the lifelong benefits of college sports. In addition, adding former professionals to rosters costs already-enrolled student-athletes valuable playing time and development opportunities during their precious years in college.

Amid this chaos, the need to pass the Protect College Sports Act is more apparent than ever. This bipartisan bill addresses the current legal instability head-on by creating one clear, fair and enforceable eligibility standard to prevent further erosion of the competitive balance that makes college sports meaningful. Crucially, the PCSA does not stop there. It also codifies important student-athlete benefits into law, including scholarship, healthcare and revenue-sharing protections. And it takes steps to protect broad opportunities, particularly in women's and Olympic sports, by establishing sport minimums and roster protections.

This balanced approach has earned the PCSA a broad consensus of support, uniting professional, Olympic and collegiate sport groups — including student-athlete leaders and conferences across all three divisions — all of whom recognize what's at stake right now for the future of college athletics.

As the Senate prepares to return from recess and the new school year begins, the urgency is higher than ever. College sports matter. They serve our nation's youth, and I believe they are the greatest human development tool in the entire world. By passing the PCSA, lawmakers can ensure they continue to benefit young generations of athletes for decades to come.

Charlie Baker is president of the NCAA.

title: ‘The league’s a disaster right now’: Mike Francesa calls out WNBA
description: It’s been a wild summer for the WNBA, between the seemingly endless controversies involving Caitlin Clark and all of the political firestorm that ensued after Sophie Cunningham spoke out against transgender women in women’s sports. While it’s certainly led to a lot of media attention, it isn’t exactly good attention. Over the past few months,…
fullText:
It's been a wild summer for the WNBA, between the seemingly endless controversies involving Caitlin Clark and all of the political firestorm that ensued after Sophie Cunningham spoke out against transgender women in women's sports. While it's certainly led to a lot of media attention, it isn't exactly good attention.

Over the past few months, the WNBA has become the most toxic space in all sports as players and the league itself have become political pawns. Now, longtime radio host Mike Francesa is calling out the league's leadership.

During his podcast this week, Mike Francesa was asked his take on the current state of the WNBA, and he was certainly not shy about blaming the WNBA's leadership for not having the foresight to see how things would change once Clark entered the league and the players for not welcoming her.

"They have turned their league into a bubbling, volcanic, political, chaotic situation where every nut is now getting involved politically in the WNBA on all different levels," Francesa ranted on his podcast. "It's the worst thing that could have ever happened. I blame the people who run the league, I blame the players who didn't have the long-range vision and didn't have the smarts to realize what Caitlin Clark was going to do for their league, and instead, tried to hurt her and run her out of the league at every point."

Francesa went on to compare Clark to when Pete Maravich joined the Atlanta Hawks.

"There were revolts against Pete Maravich when he came to the NBA," Francesa recalled. "He broke up a very good Atlanta Hawks team because there was insane jealousy and people felt he hadn't earned anything and they felt he was just a self-promoting showboat."

While the issues might have started with Clark, Francesa acknowledges that the issues are far beyond her at this point.

"Caitlin Clark came to that league and energized it in a way that they had never seen possible," Francesa added.  "They had never been able to sell that league to anybody, and she sold it to everybody. And they're all trying to ruin it. And now it's become a political mess way past just the issues with Caitlin Clark. The league's a disaster right now."

title: Family sues after 6-year-old girl dies when badminton racket shaft pierces skull
description: A New Jersey family's wrongful death lawsuit alleges Franklin Sports sold a defective badminton racket that fatally struck 6-year-old Lucy Morgan in Maine.
fullText:
The family of a 6-year-old New Jersey girl who died after a badminton racket came apart and pierced her skull during a Maine vacation is suing the Massachusetts-based maker of the sports equipment.

"This case represents a parent's worst nightmare," attorney Charles P. Hehmeyer, who is representing the family, said. "The Morgan family was enjoying an idyllic summer vacation here in Maine when they lost Lucy due to what we allege was a dangerous and defective piece of sports equipment."

The wrongful death and product-liability lawsuit alleges Franklin Sports sold a defective and unreasonably dangerous badminton racket that failed during normal use and turned its metal shaft into a projectile.

Lucy Morgan was vacationing with her parents and siblings in Limerick, Maine, on June 1, 2024, when the tragedy unfolded.

College Grad Reportedly Dies In Six Flags Roller Coaster Incident As Family Sues Theme Park

Maine State Police said Lucy's 10-year-old brother was playing outside when the aluminum shaft became dislodged from the wooden handle. The shaft struck Lucy in the head and pierced her skull, authorities said.

Lucy was taken to Southern Maine Health Care in Sanford before being airlifted to Maine Medical Center in Portland, where she died June 5, 2024, police said.

U.s. Track Star Sues Puma Team Over F1 Team-designed Gear She Says Caused Career-ending Injury

According to a copy of the complaint obtained by Fox News Digital, the Franklin badminton set had been supplied at the family's rental cottage.

The lawsuit alleges the racket's handle and metal shaft were not adequately secured, the adhesive joining the pieces was defective or insufficient, and the design lacked a secondary restraint that could have prevented the metal portion from flying free. The family also alleges Franklin Sports failed to warn consumers about the risk.

Hehmeyer told WCVB 5 that the case was not Franklin Sports' first issue involving a racket separating. He said a child in New York lost an eye when a racket came apart, and alleged the company knew of that case but failed to make a fix.

Montana Boy Killed After Being Flung From Carnival Ride Operating With Missing Restraints, Lawsuit Alleges

"The company knew that but chose not to correct this with something as simple as a pin in the handle, which would cost pennies," Hehmeyer told the outlet.

The lawsuit seeks compensatory and punitive damages, though it does not list a specific dollar figure. The family is seeking funeral expenses, emotional distress damages, loss of comfort, society and companionship, and other relief permitted under Maine law.

According to the complaint, Lucy's three siblings witnessed the incident and suffered "severe emotional distress." Her parents heard her screaming and ran to her aid, the complaint alleges.

Heartbroken Fathers Find Divine Hope In Secret Notes Left By Girls Killed In Camp Mystic Flood

Lucy's father, Jesse Morgan, a pastor at Green Pond Bible Chapel in Rockaway, New Jersey, previously wrote that the family had been spending its final full day at a lake cottage when the children decided to play badminton in the front yard.

Florida 3-Year-old Dies After Tragic Incident Involving Common Play Toy At Babysitter's House

In the days following Lucy's death, Jesse Morgan shared the faith that sustained his family through their grief. He told Fox News Digital that a friend returned Lucy's backpack after the family came home from Maine, and inside was the prayer journal she had received about a month before she died. The journal contained drawings, Bible-themed notes and messages about her belief in God, her father said.

Jesse Morgan told Fox News Digital he had no doubt Lucy "loved Christ and loved God," and that God welcomed her into heaven. He described discovering the journal as one of the "most beautiful gifts" amid the family's loss, adding that he believed his daughter had "the faith of a mustard seed."

Franklin Sports told Fox News Digital it "extends its deepest sympathies to Lucy Morgan's family and all those affected by this tragic accident."

"Because litigation is pending, we cannot comment on the specific allegations in the lawsuit," the company said. Franklin Sports added that it takes product-safety concerns "very seriously," is committed to product quality and safety, and is reviewing the circumstances surrounding the incident.

Fox News Digital reached out to attorneys for the Morgan family for comment.

Fox News Digital's Sarah Rumpf-Whitten contributed to this report.

title: Detroit Lions may face one obstacle in any Christian Gonzalez trade pursuit
description: Detroit’s defense intercepted 13 passes last season, tied for 11th in the NFL. Four of those came from cornerbacks, and D.J. Reed accounted for two of them. Carter Bahns and Zachary Pereles of CBS Sports named the Lions on Thursday among five potential landing spots for New England Patriots cornerback Christian Gonzalez, alongside the Dallas […] The post Detroit Lions may face one obstacle in any Christian Gonzalez trade pursuit appeared first on Gridiron Heroics.
fullText:
Detroit's defense intercepted 13 passes last season, tied for 11th in the NFL. Four of those came from cornerbacks, and D.J. Reed accounted for two of them.

Carter Bahns and Zachary Pereles of CBS Sports named the Lions on Thursday among five potential landing spots for New England Patriots cornerback Christian Gonzalez, alongside the Dallas Cowboys, Washington Commanders, New York Giants and Pittsburgh Steelers.

Terrion Arnold, the 24th pick of the 2024 draft, was released by Detroit in June while facing felony charges he has denied, and he agreed to terms with Seattle this month. Reed inherited the No. 1 job, and the group behind him has been shuffled and interrupted by injuries throughout camp.

Tim Twentyman wrote in the club's own training camp position preview in last month that "the Arnold release hurts Detroit's depth at the position," adding it would not surprise him if general manager Brad Holmes added to the spot before the regular season. That went up five weeks before Gonzalez's name entered the conversation, written by someone the team employs.

Detroit ranked 28th in opponent passer rating in the red zone last season at 104.3, allowing 19 passing touchdowns inside its own 20-yard line without intercepting a throw there. Reed's year split around a hamstring strain that cost him six games, and he turns 30 in November.

Gonzalez turned 24 this summer and has two seasons left on his contract. He closed 2025 with three pass breakups and four solo tackles in New England's Super Bowl LX loss to the Seahawks.

The #Lions are listed as a top landing spot for #Patriots CB Christian Gonzalez if he were to be traded Per CBS Sports pic.twitter.com/shw9ae09nF

— NFL Rumors (@nflrums) August 29, 2026

Gonzalez is playing on a rookie deal worth $4.8 million this season that runs through 2027 after New England exercised his fifth-year option in April. Detroit would inherit two years of control and an immediate negotiation, and that negotiation now starts from a number set this month in Seattle, where Devon Witherspoon signed a four-year extension averaging $33 million a season with $101 million in total guarantees and just over $59 million locked in at signing.

The draft compensation would be the cheaper half of the transaction. Bahns and Pereles made that point about the Lions specifically, writing that a long-term deal for Gonzalez would limit Detroit's flexibility at other positions and that the club can carry it only because the money would not take effect until next year.

Robert Kraft said at the start of training camp that New England had offered Gonzalez a deal that would make him the highest-paid cornerback in league history and the highest-paid player in franchise history.

"We love Christian Gonzalez," Kraft said. "We love him as a player, as a person. That's why we've made an offer to him that makes him the highest-paid player ever to play that position in the NFL, and coincidentally, it's the highest contract in the Patriots franchise history,"

Adam Schefter said on The Pat McAfee Show during the week that the sides are "obviously not in the same neighborhood right now and haven't been."

Eliot Wolf, the club's executive vice president of player personnel, answered yes this week when asked if New England still intends to reach that figure.

Gonzalez reported to camp on time and practiced in pads, passing up a holdout that would have cost him $45,000 for every day he missed. He returned to full participation this week after a hard fall on Aug. 10 kept him out of both of the Patriots' first two preseason games. Asked about the standoff, he told reporters it was "frustrating, but I'm focused on the season."

His trainer posted, then deleted, a message on Thursday saying New England should trade him. That remains the loudest anyone in Gonzalez's circle has been all summer.

The Patriots reached Super Bowl LX in February and open this season with a quarterback still on a rookie contract, which places them inside the window where a cornerback of Gonzalez's standing is worth more to them than to anyone else.

title: ‘Enes Kanter Stats’ — Sophie Cunningham’s Rough Night Vs. Sun Sees WNBA Fans Question Audacity of Fever Star’s 6th Player of the Year Case

fullText:
Sophie Cunningham has dominated nationwide headlines for over a month following her comments against trans athletes' eligibility in women's sports.

On Friday night, it was her play on the hardwood that caught basketball fans' attention. In a comfortable, 20-point win over the Connecticut Sun, Cunningham registered a single point off the bench, and fans weren't all too pleased with her performance, to say the least.

In 14 minutes of play, Cunningham dropped 1 point on 0-3 shooting from the field, along with 3 turnovers. Her single offensive contribution came from the charity stripe, and most of her damage was on the defensive end of the floor.

The WNBA world was livid as they expected more from a 'Sixth Player of the Year' candidate.

"Sophie Cunningham scored 1 point in 14 minutes for the Fever tonight. Thought I'd share these stats, since she wants us to talk about basketball now," said one user, who has been sharing her stats on X each time she underperforms.

This post alluded toCunningham's comments on August 5, "I'm going to let people just do the speaking for themselves, but for me, I want to get back to basketball. It's always been about basketball."

Another X user, whileroasting her for her 1-point stat line, wrote, "If only this grifter could hit buckets as well as point fingers. She sucks."

One WNBA observer pointed out that merely a day ago, the Fever created multiple posts to campaign for Cunningham to win the 'Sixth Player of the Year' award.

They wrote, "And the Fever has the nerve to create a 6POY for her," which was followed by numerous crying laughing emojis.

Another kept it simple and wrote, "Enes Kanter stats," alluding to the fact that Kanter, who has also been in headlines since his WNBA Draft declaration, was never a star during his 11-year NBA stint.

Last night's game saw the Fever lead by 15 points at the end of the first half. It was never truly close as Indy ran away with the 111-91 win.

So, it wasn't incumbent upon Cunningham to have a double-digit scoring night and shoot her usual, 44%+ blistering percentage from beyond the arc.

However, with the Fever making it very clear they want her to win an award for her bench role, scoring a single point certainly didn't move the needle in her favor.

In fact, the current frontrunner for the 'Sixth Player of the Year' award is the Golden State Valkyries' Janelle Salaün, who is averaging 12.9 points on 42.5% shooting from the field while holding her own on both ends of the floor against opposing bench units.

The Valkyries also hold a better record than the Fever in the standings (28-11 vs. 26-14).

With merely four games left for the Fever to play in this regular season, she would have to make quite the impression to make people forget about her 1-point performance and try to dethrone Salaün as the favorite for the award.

title: Penix Closes Gap as Falcons QB Race Boils Over
description: The gap Michael Penix Jr. and Tua Tagovailoa has been closed in the Atlanta Falcons quarterback race, according to Yahoo Sports . NFL Network insider Ian Rapoport says the lead Tagovailoa held is gone. Both players will now split first-team reps to settle the starting job. The competition is wide open and the pressure is…
fullText:
The gap Michael Penix Jr. and Tua Tagovailoa has been closed in the Atlanta Falcons quarterback race, according to Yahoo Sports. NFL Network insider Ian Rapoport says the lead Tagovailoa held is gone. Both players will now split first-team reps to settle the starting job. The competition is wide open and the pressure is on for both men.

Tagovailoa started with a huge advantage. He looked great during the offseason while Penix was stuck on the sideline. The organization wanted him to win the job and move forward as the starter. That plan relied on Penix staying injured for a while. But the knee injury healed faster than expected.

Penix needed surgery in the week of November 24, 2025, to address a partially torn ACL in his left knee. Before that hurt knee, he threw for 1,982 yards. He completed 60.1 per cent of his passes. Nine total touchdowns and three interceptions were recorded by him during the 2025 season. Now he is back and ready to fight.

Tagovailoa has not looked as sharp in the preseason. Both in practice and in games, Rapoport noted that he had been inconsistent. The gap that seemed so wide has shrunk to nothing. Rapoport explained that Tagovailoa 'had a big-time lead in this race'. That lead is under serious pressure now.

Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski confirmed the split reps. This move proves the door is open for Penix. Rapoport stated that while he seems to have been practicing better the last couple of days, the door is open for Michael Penix. That quote from Rapoport sums up the whole situation perfectly.

The coach made the call after Penix was cleared for 11-on-11 work. This means the competition can now properly begin. Both players get to show what they can do on the field. No more waiting for the injured guy to catch up. They are both in the mix right now.

Penix knows what he can do. He told reporters that as far as a pocket, he can do everything. He is confident in his skills. The only thing holding him back is his doctor's advice on taking hits. His doctor is still waiting for the point when he is comfortable with him taking hits.

That time is getting closer every day. The Falcons' quarterback decision could soon become much clearer. Fans will see the real difference between these two soon enough. The split reps are the first step in a long battle.

There is plenty at stake for Tagovailoa. He is on a one-year deal. This game could be his only chance to prove he belongs. If he loses the job, he might not have another shot in Atlanta. He needs to show he is the long-term starter in the NFL.

Penix faces his own pressure too. He spent much of training camp working his way back. He cannot afford to waste this opportunity. He needs to reclaim the starting role he appeared set to compete for before his injury. The clock is ticking for both of them.

The original plan was for Penix to rehab his knee and return when healthy. The team hoped he would just give Atlanta another option if a change was needed during the season. Now that plan is dead. The team has to pick one man to lead the offense.

Tagovailoa has struggled during the preseason. Rapoport noted that he had been inconsistent both in practice and in games. The door is open for Michael Penix to walk right in. The Falcons fans will get their answer very soon. The race has reached a boiling point.

title: ‘Transphobes are pathetic’: Transgender golfer not apologizing to ‘deeply unwell’ bigots after run of dominance

fullText:
The role of transgender athletes participating in women's sports has become one of the biggest debates in the country following Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham's comments on the matter in an ESPN profile earlier this summer.

"I got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans. And I'm like, 'I never once said that,'" Cunningham said. "I think that I am here to extend love. But I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men."

Since Cunningham's initial comments, everyone from sports media members to opposing coaches to the White House has weighed in. Now, the debate has reached Alberta, Canada. Transgender golfers Veronica Ivy and Rachel Elser have won five individual women's golf championships this summer, and aren't apologizing for it.

"To the bigots: stay mad, and get a better hobby," Ivy wrote, according to Outkick. "You're deeply unwell and you're obsessed with harassing a stranger. You're not going to make me stop existing and succeeding. I feel really sorry for you. You have my pity."

Alberta Golf updated its official policy to be more inclusive of all competitors in 2025. The organization's rules read as follows:

"For individuals who have undergone gender reassignment after puberty, the following guidelines will be used: I. Male-to-female transgendered persons, to compete as a female, must submit documentation from a medical practitioner that gender reassignment has been ongoing for at least one year."

They just see that I won some competition–without any checking for what level of competition it was," Ivy told OutSports of her detractors earlier this month. "I went from competing in elite world-level track cycling, though never making the national team or the Olympics, to contesting for age group provincial titles.

"I still haven't cracked the top 10 at the Canadian national mid-amateur championship. I'm just out here trying my best, being a good competitor. Transphobes are pathetic."

Hopefully, both Ivy and Elser will keep competing and living their lives to their fullest.

title: 49ers insider weighs in on possibility 49ers are sold by Jed York
description: NBC Sports Bay Area's Matt Maiocco's doesn't think Jed York's arrest will change the way he views the ownership of the 49ers.
fullText:
The fallout from owner Jed York's arrest continues to hang over the San Francisco 49ers, but NBC Sports Bay Area's Matt Maiocco doesn't believe it will cost the York family the franchise.

York was charged with two misdemeanors — disorderly conduct and possession of criminal tools — after responding to an undercover ad on what was described as a known prostitution website. He received a two-day jail sentence and a $1,150 fine. NFL commissioner Roger Goodell confirmed at the league's preseason owners' meeting that the incident is being reviewed under the personal conduct policy. York did not attend the meeting, a decision that wasn't surprising given how recent the arrest was.

Speaking on KNBR, Maiocco addressed the inevitable speculation about a forced sale directly, pointing to how deliberately the York family structured its ownership just two years ago.

"I can't see that. Jed bought equity from his mom in order to become the principal owner. Yes, the 49ers raised a lot of money by selling off around 9.7% of the organization, but when they transferred ownership officially over to Jed as the principal owner, the idea was this was a move made to ensure that it remained in the family," Maiocco said. "I would imagine the long-term plan is for Jed to hand it over to one of his sons or keep it in the family. I don't think this [arrest] will impact that. I think that there will be some discipline by commissioner Roger Goodell. I think it can happen sooner rather than later because the legal process has run its course. I would expect a fine and even a suspension, where he has to stay away from the team for a certain amount of time."

York became the 49ers' principal owner in March 2024, purchasing additional equity from his family specifically to formalize what had effectively been his role since taking over as CEO in 2010. At the time, York did frame the move as a long-term succession plan, saying it was "reflective of how we've operated" and intended to keep the team "in our family for generations to come." His mother, Denise DeBartolo York, and father, Dr. John York, remained co-chairs.

Maiocco acknowledged the situation is embarrassing for the organization and could become a talking point if the 49ers stumble out of the gate, but he drew a comparison to another franchise that weathered owner controversy without a sale: the New England Patriots under Robert Kraft.

"Nobody was talking about that with Robert Kraft," Maiocco said, "and I think it'll blow over, but it will always be kind of in the back of people's minds."

title: Today in sports history, September 21
description: Today in sports history, September 21
fullText:
Today is Sept. 21. On this date in:

1892: John Clarkson of the Cleveland Spiders defeated Pittsburgh 3-2 to become the fifth pitcher in major league history to reach 300 career victories.

1896: Connie Mack announced he would leave Pittsburgh to manage Milwaukee in the Western League, a career move that preceded his legendary tenure as an owner and executive with the Athletics.

1933: The Washington Senators defeated the St. Louis Browns 2-1 to clinch the American League pennant.

1934: St. Louis Cardinals rookie Paul "Daffy" Dean pitched a no-hitter in a 3-0 victory over the Brooklyn Dodgers, completing a doubleheader sweep after his brother Dizzy Dean threw a three-hit shutout in the opener.

1955: Rocky Marciano recovered from a second-round knockdown and stopped Archie Moore in the ninth round at Yankee Stadium to retain the heavyweight championship. Marciano retired the following year with a 49-0 record.

1961: The Minnesota Twins defeated the Washington Senators 6-3 in the final major league game at Griffith Stadium in Washington.

1963: Pittsburgh Pirates coach Gene Baker became the first Black person to take charge of a major league team when he managed the final two innings after manager Danny Murtaugh and coach Frank Oceak were ejected against the Los Angeles Dodgers.

1969: New York Jets punter Steve O'Neal launched a 98-yard punt against the Denver Broncos, setting an NFL record that still stands.

1970: The Cleveland Browns defeated the New York Jets 31-21 in the inaugural "Monday Night Football" regular-season telecast on ABC.

1971: American League owners approved the relocation of the Washington Senators to Arlington, Texas, clearing the way for the franchise that became the Texas Rangers.

1978: San Diego Padres pitcher Gaylord Perry defeated the San Francisco Giants 5-1 for his 20th victory, reaching the mark for the fifth time in his career.

1981: Philadelphia Phillies pitcher Steve Carlton struck out 12 Montreal Expos and surpassed Bob Gibson as the National League's career strikeout leader.

1982: NFL players began a strike that suspended the season for 57 days and reduced each team's schedule from 16 games to nine.

1985: Michael Spinks defeated Larry Holmes by unanimous decision in Las Vegas to capture the heavyweight championship and end Holmes' undefeated reign.

1990: Oakland's Bob Welch became the first major league pitcher in 12 years to reach 25 victories in a season.

2001: In the first major sporting event in New York after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, Mike Piazza hit a dramatic eighth-inning home run to lift the Mets past the Atlanta Braves 3-2 at Shea Stadium.

2008: The New York Yankees defeated the Baltimore Orioles 7-3 in the final game at the original Yankee Stadium, which had opened in 1923.

2008: The United States defeated Europe 16½-11½ at Valhalla Golf Club to win the Ryder Cup and snap a streak of three consecutive European victories.

2014: Lewis Hamilton won the Singapore Grand Prix and took the Formula One championship lead while equaling Juan Manuel Fangio's mark of eight Grand Prix victories for Mercedes.

2019: Manchester City defeated Watford 8-0 for the largest top-flight victory in club history and became the first Premier League team to lead 5-0 after 18 minutes.

2024: The Chicago White Sox lost their 119th game, tying the 2003 Detroit Tigers' American League record for losses in a season.

title: Tony Romo receives 3 new citations following OWI arrest in Milwaukee
description: Romo is due in court on Sept. 21. It's unclear if he'll call games for CBS Sports again.
fullText:
Tony Romo has received three new citations stemming from his arrest in Milwaukee on suspicion of operating a vehicle while intoxicated, according to the Milwaukee Journal-Sentinel.

According to online court records, the former Dallas Cowboys quarterback and current CBS Sports analyst was cited for first-offense operating while intoxicated, unsafe passing on the right side and possessing open intoxicants in his vehicle. Romo had already received a citation on July 27 for refusing to take an intoxication test after his arrest.

Romo is reportedly due in court for all four citations on Sept. 21.

His camp also released a new statement to the Journal-Sentinel:

"Tony accepts full responsibility for his actions and has taken proactive steps to ensure that this isolated civil matter is properly resolved. We are working with local authorities to bring this matter to a close and we are communicating with CBS about next steps."

Romo was arrested on July 23 after being pulled over on a Milwaukee highway and performing poorly on a field sobriety test, according to police.

In addition to legal repercussions, Romo was soon placed on indefinite leave by CBS Sports. His future with the network remains uncertain, with company president David Berson declining to provide a timetable for a final decision while speaking with reporters earlier this month.

Romo was once the darling of NFL media and CBS paid him like it with a record-shattering 10-year, $180 million contract in 2020. His luster had worn off considerably even before the arrest, with his meandering and casual commentary style wearing thin for many fans.

So it might not be a surprise if CBS uses the arrest to get out of that contract and cut Romo loose. The Athletic noted his contract contains a morals clause that could allow CBS to void the deal if he embarrasses the company.

In the meantime, CBS is set to open the season with J.J. Watt working opposite Jim Nantz in its No. 1 booth.

description: Olympic champion Alysa Liu will sit out the 2026-27 figure skating season, taking another break from competition while continuing to train ahead of a planned return the following year.  “I always want to challenge myself in new ways, so my artistry and skating can evolve,” Liu wrote.  Liu told NBC Sports that she intends to continue working with her longtime Bay Area coaches, Phillip DiGuglielmo and Massimo Scali, with an emphasis on her “overall artistry, spins, jumps, everything”.
fullText:
Olympic champion Alysa Liu will sit out the 2026-27 figure skating season, taking another break from competition while continuing to train ahead of a planned return the following year.

The 21-year-old American announced her decision on social media, saying she wanted time to "recalibrate" and develop her skating away from the demands of competition.

"I always want to challenge myself in new ways, so my artistry and skating can evolve," Liu wrote. "It's important to me that my sport reflects my personal growth."

Liu told NBC Sports that she intends to continue working with her longtime Bay Area coaches, Phillip DiGuglielmo and Massimo Scali, with an emphasis on her "overall artistry, spins, jumps, everything".

"I really want to improve my skating, and I wanted to take the time to do that for myself and just to evolve," she said. "And then I'll be back after that is done."

The decision represents another unconventional turn in a career that has carried Liu from child prodigy to burnout, retirement and an unlikely return as world and Olympic champion.

Liu became the youngest ever US women's champion aged 13, when her 4ft 6in frame left her too short to reach the top of the podium without help from the other medalists. But the relentless training and attention that accompanied her rapid ascent gradually drained her enthusiasm for the sport.

She retired at 16, only months after finishing sixth in her Olympic debut at the 2022 Beijing Games, and later described how comprehensively she had come to reject the life built around her skating.

"I really hated skating when I quit," Liu said in the run-up to the Milano Cortina Olympics. "I didn't care about competitions. I didn't care about places. I didn't care about skaters. I didn't care about my programs. I just wanted to get away."

Liu enrolled at UCLA, studied psychology and went hiking in the Himalayas with friends while discovering an identity beyond the rink. Her desire to skate returned unexpectedly during a ski trip to Lake Tahoe, where gliding down the mountain rekindled her love of movement.

She began skating once a week at public sessions in El Segundo, California, and found that the difficult jumps that had propelled her childhood rise had not entirely deserted her. Liu eventually decided to mount a comeback, but only with greater control over her career, including her music, costumes, diet and training schedule.

The results would no longer define the experience, she insisted. Her initial ambition was simply to make another Olympic team and use the sport as a form of self-expression.

That approach carried Liu to a surprise world championship in 2025, making her the first American woman to win the title since Kimmie Meissner in 2006. In February, she landed seven clean triple jumps to rise from third place after the short program and win the Olympic women's singles title in Milan.

The West Oakland native became the first American woman to claim the event since Sarah Hughes in 2002. She also won gold in the Olympic team competition.

"Really the only word that comes to mind when I think about my entire journey is grateful," Liu told NBC Sports. "I think the reason why it's been so fun is because I have my own agency. I really like to skate, and so that's why I skate."

Liu said she assessed her emotional and physical state earlier this summer and concluded that stepping away was the right choice. DiGuglielmo and Scali supported the decision.

"Logically and emotionally and physically, this just makes the most sense," she told NBC Sports. "I will miss seeing the international competitors at all the international competitions, but there will be more, so it's fine."

A rush of opportunities followed Liu's Olympic victory. Nearly 5,000 people turned out for a homecoming celebration in her honor, where Oakland mayor Barbara Lee presented her with a key to the city. She withdrew from the world championships in March, performed alongside her Olympic teammates on the Stars on Ice tour, attended Louis Vuitton's Paris Fashion Week show and wore the label to the Met Gala.

Liu had been scheduled to compete at Skate America from 13-15 November in Everett, Washington.

title: Why does college football generate so many Freezing Cold Takes?
description: Fred Segal is no different than a lot of fans. When he was an attorney, he would consume sports takes just like anyone else: scrolling Twitter, watching ESPN, and listening to the radio. Mostly, he accepted the bold opinions and predictions for what they were — entertainment. But there was one thing that always got…
fullText:
Fred Segal is no different than a lot of fans. When he was an attorney, he would consume sports takes just like anyone else: scrolling Twitter, watching ESPN, and listening to the radio.

Mostly, he accepted the bold opinions and predictions for what they were — entertainment. But there was one thing that always got under Fred's skin. He hated watching or listening to these pundits pat themselves on the back when one of their bold takes came to fruition.

"I'd see a reporter make a prediction about a team and that team lost, and I'd be like, 'oh, that guy was wrong,'" he told Awful Announcing in an interview. "Then he'd say the same thing the next week about another team, and that team lost, or he'd say something about a player that was going to be great, and then they weren't.

"I'd remember those and then later on that same guy would say something like, 'just like I predicted five days ago, this happened,' and I'd be like, 'Hang on! I can remember three off the top of my head where you were dead wrong. You didn't post those!'"

That is how Freezing Cold Takes was born, and it didn't take long for it to become one of the Twitter feeds every sports fan had to follow.

"I started doing it for fun," Segal said. "Just a troll type thing, maybe."

Those followers wanted to do so much of Segal's research for him, and that troll grew into a real business. Last week, Segal released his second book. Freezing Cold Takes: College Football catalogs plenty of nonsensical opinions and plenty of predictions that turned out to be very, very wrong.

Writing the book was a business opportunity, but it also gave Segal a chance to put some of the best misfires down on paper. That's pretty valuable when your brand was built on the unstable foundations of social media. Plus, it was easy, a pleasure even, for Segal.

Research for the book combined two of his favorite things: reading old newspaper articles and talking about college football. Segal keeps an eye on all sports takes, but as an SEC alum, his radar is always up for college football. It's his favorite sport, and it's the sport that might most consistently give him material.

"The emotion and the passion, nothing beats it," he says. "Everybody takes it so personally. Even in terms of the writers and TV personalities, every game creates a narrative about who is going to the playoff or what coach has to be fired after his second loss."

I asked Segal if he knew who was featured the most in Freezing Cold Takes: College Football. He didn't have the official stats handy, but his guess was either former CBS and Bleacher Report writer Barrett Sallee, OutKick founder Clay Travis, or Yahoo's Dan Wolken.

To be fair to them, though, in 2022, Segal told Dan Patrick that he had to stop tracking Skip Bayless's and Colin Cowherd's missed predictions because they were dominating the Freezing Cold Takes Twitter feed. Had he not made that decision, he may have been able to fill a whole book with just misfires from those two men.

Social media is a tricky thing now. Gauging what value your idea would have in a different environment is hard too. Maybe that's why Segal is quick to point out that he probably would have been beaten to the punch when I ask how he thinks Freezing Cold Takes would have fared if he had launched in 2025 instead of 2015.

He does note that maybe niche content isn't as valuable on social media as it used to be.

"Some very basic concepts on Twitter now work. I'll see something and think, 'oh, this is pretty basic,' and then it just blows up. I can't even tell anymore what people like and what they don't with social media."

People that have been in the sports talk game for a long time know Segal's work. Even if some privately hate it, in public, everyone will say that they know it's all in good fun. They may even say they welcome the occasional heat check.

In my years writing about sports media, though, I have had the chance to talk to students in high schools and universities across the South, and I've been shocked by what a lot of them have to say about Freezing Cold Takes.

So many people in the very early days of their careers view being highlighted by Segal's social media channels as a credibility killer. That was never what Segal intended.

"I don't think it really diminishes credibility. If anything, I think that credibility is already diminished the second a fan reads something they don't like," he says, pointing out how easy it is now for fans to find the exact opinion about their team that they want to read and believe.

Hot takes are a vital part of this industry. Sports talk is the entertainment business, after all. The stakes of what Wolken, Travis, Sallee, Cowherd, and Bayless think will happen just aren't that high. Isn't being interesting what matters most? Being right should just be a bonus.

"The ones who take [Freezing Cold Takes] seriously, I've come to realize they believe that they are doing work that's important," Segal says. "Whether it's covering a team or breaking stories, they are doing important stuff, and they work long and hard to do it. Then I come along, pass around one bad thing, and everyone laughs about it."

Segal has built a thriving business for himself, but there's no mission to the work. The community he has created is there for comedy purposes just as much as sports ones. Are you worried about seeing your name or take show up in his Twitter feed? Then you are, to borrow a phrase, hustling backward.

"It doesn't matter, right? Like, nobody's ever been fired for bad predictions ever. I mean, I can't even think of one."

title: Santos FC adds 700,000m² site for new academy training ground

fullText:
Santos FC has taken an important step toward expanding its sports infrastructure by acquiring a plot of land of approximately 700,000 square meters in São Vicente, intended for the development of the new Youth Academy Training Center. The acquisition was made possible through an agreement signed with Saint-Gobain, a long-standing commercial partner of the Club, in exchange for commercial and advertising properties.

The negotiation was supported by the City Hall of São Vicente to complete the operation, reinforcing joint efforts in favor of the municipality's development.

"First of all, it is essential to highlight the asset-related importance of this transaction with Saint-Gobain for Santos. It is an area of around 700,000 square meters, and its acquisition represents an important step for the project of the new youth academy training center. Certainly, in the future, we will use this area to expand and modernize the Club's sports infrastructure. Undeniably, this is a milestone for the current management and for Santos FC," said president Marcelo Teixeira.

"We have a historic relationship with Santos and see this agreement as another step in that journey. We believe in the transformative role of sport in society and are confident that this partnership will contribute to the club's future projects. For Saint-Gobain, this is another step in strengthening a relationship that has remained solid over the years," commented Gustavo Siqueira, Vice President of HR and Public Affairs for Saint-Gobain in Latin America.

"It is a great joy to see this transaction succeed. First, because São Vicente is undergoing strong development, especially the Continental Area, where 150,000 people live and which will receive the VLT in the coming years, creating a major development corridor. Second, because Santos Futebol Clube is a global brand, the club where King Pelé played, where Prince Neymar plays, and which will now have the opportunity to see its future and its talents develop on the lands of Brazil's First City. The City Hall of São Vicente, anticipating the legal and environmental issues necessary for the use of the area, after talks with CETESB, requested that the EIA-RIMA be commissioned. This request was granted and will allow projects to be developed in the region while respecting the environment and ensuring the proper use of the area by the club," declared the mayor of São Vicente, Kayo Amado.

The next steps related to the development of the new sports complex include carrying out the applicable environmental studies and procedures, including the process before CETESB and obtaining the necessary licenses and authorizations.

To make the construction of the new training center feasible, Santos FC is working on structuring a specific investment fund to finance the implementation of the project. The model is under development and will be presented after the project's technical consolidation.

title: Drought leaves sports clubs 'praying for rain'
description: Some grass pitches are dry and hard and clubs are struggling to water their playing surfaces.
fullText:
Periods of drought and prolonged hot, dry weather has had a major effect on sports clubs across south-west England, who are feeling the strain.

The unprecedented weather has left some grass pitches extremely dry and hard for clubs with little to no irrigation, with many dependent on meaningful rainfall for recovery.

A hosepipe ban was put in force on 9 August across Devon, Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly as the conditions put "significant pressure" on the regions water supplies.

South West Water said sports pitches and surfaces were "exempt from hosepipe bans where watering is necessary", so long as it took place outside peak hours of 08:00-10:00 BST and 17:00-21:00 BST.

Bill Martin, chairman and assistant groundsman at Plymouth Cricket Club, said he had "never seen the pitch so dry".

He said this summer has been particularly difficult as a groundsman because "it had been a summer of two halves".

He said the first six weeks it was "very very wet" but since then it had been two months without significant rain.

"We've got one tap and one hose, so the real challenge has been getting water on to the surface, particularly the playing wickets.

He said without water, the ground became very dry and the grass disappeared and turned to dust, which was both difficult to play and dangerous.

"Cricket is a fine weather sport, so we've not had interruptions, we've not lost any games and we've been able to play a lot of cricket in the sunshine which has been great, but in terms of actually looking after the ground and preparing decent pitches to play on, it makes it very hard work."

"Unusually for cricketers we have been praying for rain."

The Rugby Football Union (RFU) announced the start of the community rugby season had been delayed until 21 September because of concerns about player welfare and pitch conditions. While the Football Association issued guidance which said there was "no blanket suspension of football on dry grass pitches" but the priority was to keep "football playing safely".

Lynton Football Club made the decision to postpone their opening fixture of the season.

In a post on social media the club said three players had suffered "serious injuries", with two "undoubtedly" because of the hard surfaces and would not risk any further injuries on a "rock hard almost concrete like pitch".

Nick Rich from Saltash Rugby Football Club said he had "never seen the pitch as parched as it is at the moment".

"It's rock solid out there. If you turned the tables and it was frozen in winter, you would not play a game of rugby on it."

He said the decision to delay the season was a good thing for both rugby and safety but did mean there was a delay in revenue for the club.

Just 15 months ago the club reseeded the pitch at great cost.

He said further reseeding took place earlier this summer and they had "waited for rain so the grass seed would germinate and we haven't had it yet".

"There's been some watering going on but clearly nowhere enough and we've put thousands of gallons on it."

It is a similar story at Ivybridge Bowls Club who have "struggled to keep up" with the amount of watering required during the high temperatures.

Malcolm Johnson, club captain and groundsman, said the club's watering system was small and the green should be watered at least four times a day to keep it growing, but was unable to do that because of the hosepipe restrictions imposed.

"We've got to a point now where we have to leave it as it is and are going to have to start from scratch again in the spring."

A small amount of rain caused a game to be called off on Wednesday because the water was not draining away quickly enough.

Johnson said "the surface is that hard that it is not being absorbed - we would like to spike it, we've got all the machinery to do that but it's just too hard".

title: Good Sports: Merced teens leave home to pursue pro soccer dreams
description: Leaving home to follow a dream. That's what both Immanuel Ewing and Jorge Salmeron did at just 13 and 14 years old. The boys signed MLS Next Pro contracts with Crew 2.
fullText:
Leaving home to follow a dream.

"At first, it was hard leaving my family," says Jorge Salmeron.

That's what both Immanuel Ewing and Jorge Salmeron did at just 13 and 14 years old.

"It's super hard, especially the first year," Ewing said.

"Leaving your family behind, your siblings behind, but he's definitely willing to make that sacrifice and work hard for it," says Mariana Rivera, Ewing's mother.

Both Immanuel and Jorge grew up playing soccer in Merced with Albion SC.

To reach their goal of the pros, the two made a sacrifice: leave home and join an MLS developmental academy.

"We see them competing at the highest level," says Albion SC Coach Rafael Valencia. "You see it in the intensity they bring in practice."

The Merced kids found their way to Columbus, Ohio, earning a spot with the Columbus Crew Academy.

Each has made appearances with Crew 2, the last step before becoming a pro.

In the inaugural MLS Next Cup, Immanuel won the MVP award for the U-19 championship.

"It's definitely something I didn't think I would end up getting," he said. "I never thought I would be able to achieve something like that."

Now, both Immanuel and Jorge are making more than just an appearance.

The boys signed MLS Next Pro contracts with Crew 2.

"It's just something you've been wanting for your whole life," Jorge said.

The Crew franchise gains two Valley natives after losing one in July.

Fresno native Max Arfsten was picked by the Crew in the 2023 MLS SuperDraft, won an MLS Cup with the team before being named to the U-S men's national team roster and debuting in the 2026 FIFA World Cup.

Max is on his way to the English Championship side with Middlesbrough FC, passing the reins to Immanuel and Jorge to represent the Valley here in the States.

"All the hard work is finally paying off," Jorge said. "It's just a small step to keep pushing forward."

"For all the little kids out here, kind of just give them something to look up to," Immanuel said. "Show them that there's stuff outside of Merced. It's not just this small town. You can do whatever you put your mind to."

title: Bill Rasmussen Had A Crazy Idea. It Became ESPN
description: Bill Rasmussen turned an improbable idea into ESPN, reshaping sports television and leaving a legacy that endured long after he lost control of the network he founded.
fullText:
In August 1978, Bill Rasmussen was stuck in traffic on Interstate 84 with his son, Scott, trying to solve a problem: They had plans for a sports cable network and enough satellite capacity to cover 8,760 hours a year. What could possibly fill all that time?

Scott offered an answer that sounded almost absurd: play sports all day.

From that traffic jam emerged the blueprint for what became the Entertainment and Sports Programming Network, soon known by its initialism, ESPN.

That brainstorm established Rasmussen, who died Aug. 18 at 93 from the effects of Parkinson's disease, as a founding father of around-the-clock sports television and helped change how generations of fans consumed sports.

"He had an idea, and he had a dream," Bob Rauscher, who launched NFL GameDay in 1985, said. "And he made it happen."

Rasmussen's broadcasting career began in western Massachusetts in the 1960s, before he became communications director for the New England Whalers of the World Hockey Association. After being fired alongside the entire Whalers front office in 1978, Rasmussen began exploring the possibility of creating a cable sports operation of his own.

His original concept was a local Connecticut cable channel that could carry University of Connecticut basketball games, following the model of MSG in New York and WGN in Chicago, according to Vince Doria, ESPN's now-retired vice president for news.

Rasmussen was reminded that once the signal was sent to the satellite, it could be received well beyond Connecticut. That realization expanded the possibilities dramatically, Doria said, even though not everyone saw the idea's merit.

"Everybody thought it was a nuts idea at the time," Doria said

Rasmussen had already incorporated E.S.P. Network when the idea crystallized during that August 1978 road trip, he recalled in a 2012 Forbes interview.

"Scott finally said something like, 'Play football all day, for all I care,' and suddenly, the ideas started coming fast and furious during that car ride," Rasmussen recalled in that interview. "We came up with the idea for 'Sports Center,' we had designed the entire building we would be in, we had decided what types of sports we should go after.

"That car ride was where we hung the heavy steel work for the network."

The Entertainment and Sports Programming Network set up shop on land Rasmussen bought in Bristol, Connecticut, and launched with its opening show, SportsCenter, at 7 p.m. on Sept. 7, 1979, available in about 1.4 million cable households.

Rauscher said the concept of a channel devoted to sports highlights and coverage far beyond the three-minute local news segment was unprecedented, making it a "sports fan's dream."

"I think [Rasmussen] understood that there was this appetite there," Rauscher, who came to ESPN in August 1980, said. "There would be this allegiance and loyalty to want to consume that much material."

It also came with challenges. Few people had cable when the network launched and many that did were confused by the network's name, Doria said. Securing enough programming was another challenge, forcing ESPN to fill portions of its schedule with Australian rules football and even circus events.

Rasmussen also had to persuade a trio of constituencies that didn't yet know they needed round-the-clock sports on television: investors to finance it, sports organizations to provide games and advertisers to believe somebody would watch.

Rasmussen parlayed his own $9,000 credit-card advance and $75,000 in financing arranged through K.S. Sweet into the fledgling venture. Stuart Evey, who oversaw who oversaw Getty Oil's investments outside its core oil business, persuaded the company's board to invest $10 million for an 85% stake. Anheuser-Busch signed on as an advertiser with what was then the largest single advertising buy in cable history.

"Bill was the one that sought the financing," Doria said. "He was the one that chased the NCAA. He got the property in Bristol. He made the deal with RCA.

Taking Getty's money, however, also meant surrendering control.

As ESPN prepared to launch, Evey decided to bring on more experienced television management in the form of Chet Simmons, president of NBC Sports. Simmons became ESPN president in July 1979. Rasmussen was moved to chairman, effectively stripping him of day-to-day authority.

Rasmussen left his active role at ESPN in 1980 and remained largely disconnected from the company until then-president George Bodenheimer welcomed him back for ESPN's 20th anniversary in 1999.

"He was gone so quickly," Doria said. "He wasn't there for the heyday of when it really became successful and a household name.

"But without his initiative, perseverance and determination, it doesn't happen. "

Steve Anderson was trying to follow his Pulitzer Prize-winning father, Dave Anderson, into the sports media game when he read about a little cable company in Connecticut that was "hiring anybody."

"I never thought this thing was going to make it," Anderson said. "I was only hoping that it was going to last long enough so I could get some experience and go back to New York, and get a real job at a real network."

ESPN instead became Anderson's professional home for more than three decades, and he credits Rasmussen with helping establish the family culture that defined its early years.

"Many of us who were there back in the '80s and '90s, we talk about the bond that we all had, the camaraderie we all have just being a part of that team," he said, "because we weren't sure ESPN was going to make it."

Rasmussen remained an entrepreneur after leaving ESPN, and advised the Big Ten on television strategy and pursuing several early internet sports ventures. He also spent decades telling the story of ESPN's unlikely creation through speeches and books, culminating in the 2026 documentary and book Sports Heaven: The Birth of ESPN.

He learned he had Parkinson's disease in 2014 and publicly revealed the diagnosis in 2019. He later became an ambassador for the Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Research and joined its Patient Council.

Even as his health declined and he used a wheelchair, Rasmussen continued gathering in Florida with retired ESPN veterans.

"He always made you feel like he knew you and appreciated what you did for ESPN and everything else," said Anderson. "He was remarkable in that way."

There was, however, a bittersweet element to Rasmussen's relationship with the company he created. He was pushed aside so early that he missed being part of ESPN's emergence as a sports-media powerhouse, Anderson said.

"He never even experienced the early successes of ESPN," he said. "As I got to know him a little bit and got to see him and listen to him talk, I always felt sad for him that he never really experienced the real success of ESPN firsthand."

Yet Anderson said Rasmussen eventually received the respect such an accomplishment deserved. When he attended ESPN alumni gatherings later in life, he was routinely approached by people seeking to express their gratitude.

"Everybody who had been there at ESPN was going up to him thanking him," Anderson said. "Because he was such a humble man and such a nice man, it was easy for everybody to do."
